one_liner: Pure-Go (CGO=0) RGBA resizer whose multicore Bicubic/Lanczos beat single-thread Pillow 12.2 1.7-4.9x; its serial Box loses.
what_it_does: The resample package of go-gfx resizes straight-alpha 8-bit RGBA raster.Image buffers with Nearest, Bilinear, Box (area), Bicubic (Keys a=-0.5) and Lanczos (a=3) filters. The API is two functions, Resize(src, w, h, mode) and ResizePremultiplied(src, w, h, mode), returning a new *raster.Image; standard-library images go in and out through raster.FromImage and ToRGBA. Bicubic and Lanczos port Pillow's precompute_coeffs scheme (filter footprint widened by the reduction factor) so output tracks Pillow at 42.7-61.2 dB PSNR.
how_it_is_fast: Bicubic and Lanczos are separable: a horizontal gather pass writes a float64 scratch plane, then the vertical pass builds each output row as one axpy (dst += w*src) per filter tap over a whole contiguous RGBA row, run by go-asmgen assembly kernels (arm64 NEON VFMLA, amd64 SSE2 MULPD+ADDPD, s390x vector). Both passes split their rows into contiguous bands, one goroutine per band up to GOMAXPROCS, once rows x output width reaches ParThreshold (16384). Most of the measured win is that fan-out: Box, which runs a serial scalar float64 weighted span sum with no SIMD and no tiling, is 0.65-0.77x Pillow.
when_to_use: Go services built with CGO disabled that need Pillow-quality Bicubic or Lanczos thumbnails or enlargements without linking libvips or Pillow.
Multi-core machines with spare cores per request: the 1.66-4.9x wins come from tiling both passes across GOMAXPROCS goroutines (16 logical CPUs in the published run).
Images large enough to cross ParThreshold (16384 output elements per pass, about a 128x128 output), e.g. 1024x1024 to 256x256 or 256x256 to 1024x1024.
Pipelines that must stay numerically close to an existing Python/Pillow pipeline: parity_test.go checks 42.7-61.2 dB premultiplied-space PSNR against Pillow 12 references.
Cut-out images with transparency, via ResizePremultiplied, which removes the colour fringe that straight-alpha filtering leaves.
when_not_to_use: Box/area downscaling or enlargement: serial and unvectorised, 0.65x (1024 to 256) and 0.77x (256 to 1024) of Pillow's speed.

Single-core containers, GOMAXPROCS=1, or servers already running one resize per core: no single-thread numbers are published. Rough estimate (not measured): Bicubic 1024 to 256 does about 4x the multiply-adds of Box (16 taps per axis versus 4), and serial Box already takes 3.53 ms, so a single-thread Bicubic run is likely behind Pillow's 3.14 ms. `go test -bench Resize -cpu 1` would settle it.
Small thumbnails: a pass below ParThreshold (e.g. a 64x64 output's vertical pass) runs serially.
Bit-exact Pillow output: go-gfx stays in float64 while Pillow uses 22-bit fixed-point integers with an 8-bit intermediate, and Box has no Pillow parity test at all (only a self-consistency test).

Memory-tight or mature-dependency settings: the scratch plane is srcH x dstW x 4 float64 (8 MiB in both benchmark cases), allocated per call; the repo dates from 2026-08-28 with 0 stars and no tagged releases.

integration.dependencies: resample imports only go-gfx's own color and raster packages; the module's go.mod also requires golang.org/x/image, sergeymakinen/go-ico, go-images/jpeg2000 and tannevaled/gobig2 (for the codec package), despite the README's 'no third-party dependencies'
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.26.4 (go.mod 'go 1.26.4'); CI also runs Go stable
integration.platforms: any Go target; SIMD axpy kernel on amd64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and s390x (vector); scalar loop plus multicore tiling on loong64, ppc64le, riscv64, 386 and arm (CI runs these under qemu)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; Resize and ResizePremultiplied allocate their own output and scratch per call and share only the package-level var ParThreshold, which tests mutate

gotchas: Resize filters all four channels independently (straight alpha), while Pillow's Image.resize converts RGBA to RGBa (premultiplied) and back for every non-NEAREST filter; ResizePremultiplied is the Pillow-equivalent call. The benchmark times Resize, and the uncommitted Pillow harness does not say whether Pillow got RGBA (and so paid both conversion passes, the second over the full 1024x1024 output on enlargement).

docs/perf.md calls Pillow's resampler 'single-threaded C with SIMD' and its BOX 'hand-tuned SIMD C'. Stock Pillow's src/libImaging/Resample.c (main branch) has no SIMD intrinsics: it is a scalar fixed-point convolution (PRECISION_BITS 22), and BOX goes through the same generic convolution as BICUBIC with support 0.5. Pillow-SIMD, the SIMD fork, was not tested.
raster.Image is straight-alpha with stride 4*W, unlike the standard library's premultiplied image.RGBA, so going through FromImage and ToRGBA adds a conversion pass that the benchmark does not time.
The amd64 kernel is SSE2 multiply-then-add (no FMA, no AVX2); TestAxpyMatchesScalar allows a small tolerance for GOAMD64=v3 builds, where the scalar fallback uses fused multiply-add.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over rez (bamiaux/rez, the other pure-Go SIMD resizer, measured only against ImageMagick and Go resizers) when you want Pillow-matching Bicubic/Lanczos output and multicore tiling built in. Pick fast_image_resize (Rust, single-thread AVX2/NEON wins over libvips) or stb-image-resize-opt and tir (C) when you are not on Go or need a single-thread speed win that has been measured.
verified_claims_summary: On an unnamed Apple Silicon Mac (16 logical CPUs), Go 1.26.4 `go test -bench` resizing random opaque RGBA images beat Pillow 12.2.0 Image.resize (best of 30) 1.66x (Bicubic) and 1.72x (Lanczos) for 1024x1024 to 256x256, and 4.9x and 3.2x for 256x256 to 1024x1024. Box lost 0.65x and 0.77x. go-gfx tiled the filtered modes across all cores against single-thread Pillow; Box was serial on both sides. The Pillow timing script is not committed.
status_note: Active (57 commits from 2026-08-28 to 2026-10-01, CI on six 64-bit architectures plus 32-bit, 2 open issues, neither about resample) and BSD-3-Clause, but brand new, with 0 stars and no releases. Its stated consumers are the same author's go-images, go-widgets and go-webengine.
